extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific method; philosophers of science; working scientists interested in methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for using and judging the Deductive Method in science: how to obtain premises by induction, perform ratiocination, and verify deductions; and how laws of nature can be explained (resolved) into other laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-part structure of the Deductive Method
rubrics_metrics.description: The Deductive Method has three essential components — Induction (to ascertain the laws of the causes), Ratiocination (to determine, from the laws of the causes, what effect a given combination of those causes will produce), and Verification (to compare the deductive conclusions with observations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All three parts must be present for deductions to have more value than guess-work. The text repeatedly stresses that Induction furnishes premisses, Ratiocination carries out the calculation/deduction, and Verification is needed to warrant reliance on conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction must supply sound premises from appropriate instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction must furnish the premises to the Deductive Method by observing appropriate instances (simple, well-eliminated cases) and establishing empirical laws (often by Method of Agreement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is important that as many empirical laws as possible be ascertained and that phenomena be described 'in the most comprehensive as well as accurate manner possible' — collecting from observation of parts the simplest correct expression for wholes (examples: planetary places, epicycles → ellipse). Avoid relying on complex instances for discovery without first obtaining simpler, eliminative instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratiocination should deduce effects from known causal laws but recognize mathematical limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Once laws of causes are known, ratiocination (calculation/rational deduction) is used to determine what effects will follow from any given combination of causes; this often requires theorems of number and geometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of practical limits: even when causes and their numerical laws are known, combining many causes may exceed mathematical ability (examples: three-body gravitation problem, projectile motion with air density, powder, etc.). Claim numerical deduction only where the necessary numerical laws and feasible calculations exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification: deductive conclusions must accord with direct observation
rubrics_metrics.description: To warrant reliance upon general conclusions reached by deduction, these conclusions must be found, 'on a careful comparison, to accord with the results of direct observation wherever it can be had.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If experience confirms deductions, they may be trusted in other cases; but if deductions predict an effect that does not occur where the same combination of causes existed, one must show (or plausibly surmise) what frustrated it, or else regard the theory as imperfect. Verification is incomplete unless some confirming cases are of at least equal complexity to cases where the theory will be applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: A good theory should deductively account for empirical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The most effectual verification is that the theory, when deduced from causes, leads to empirical laws already furnished by direct observation (e.g., Newtonian theory leading to Kepler's laws).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a theory deductively reproduces observed uniformities (complete or approximate), that is strong evidence the proposed causes really produce the phenomena. Use existing empirical laws as key tests for new theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex instances are valuable for verification but less so for discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex instances, while often not useful in discovering simple laws (because of many interacting causes), are valuable as tests that can confirm a law once discovered by simpler means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complex case that accords with a deduced law becomes a new experiment on the law and can expose previously overlooked circumstances (example: discrepancy in calculated vs observed velocity of sound revealed heat from condensation). Scientists should use complex cases to strengthen or falsify theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation by resolution into component causes and collocations
rubrics_metrics.description: One mode of explaining a law of an effect is to resolve it into the laws of the separate causes which contribute to it, together with the fact of their coexistence (collocation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explanation must specify not only the simpler laws of causation but also the collocations — the existence and relative amounts of the contributing agents (example: explaining planetary motion requires laws of rectilineal inertia and centripetal force plus their coexistence and proportions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation by identification of intermediate (proximate) causes
rubrics_metrics.description: A second mode is resolving a remote sequence A → C into an intermediate chain A → B → C; i.e., detecting intermediate phenomena that transmit causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanations should seek proximate causes and intermediate links where further observation indicates them (examples: touch → nerve-change → sensation; acid → separation of elements → charring). Recognizing intermediates yields laws that are more general and more reliable than remote generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation by subsumption under a more general law
rubrics_metrics.description: The third mode is subsuming several specific laws under one more general law that includes them all (gathering up partial laws into a general law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To subsume correctly, show that similar phenomena agree not only qualitatively but quantitatively under the same rules (example: terrestrial gravity and celestial central force subsumed under universal gravitation). This often requires combining observations from different domains to eliminate special circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer more general (simpler) laws where possible because they are more reliable
rubrics_metrics.description: When a law is resolved into more immediate or simpler laws, those simpler laws are laws of greater generality and are less likely to require limitation by subsequent experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that complex laws (laws of combined causes or remote sequences) are more liable to failure because they depend on more contingencies; therefore, scientific practice values arriving at simpler, more general laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate contingent circumstances to test universality
rubrics_metrics.description: To arrive at truly general laws, it is necessary to eliminate particular circumstances that might confound inference (e.g., proximity to Earth in early gravity observations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observations from different times, places, and observers to eliminate accidental conditions; combining multiple sets of instances helps show the law holds under more general conditions or universally.

rubrics_metrics.name: A theoretical explanation may trade one unexplained mystery for another; do not mistake explanation for ultimate why
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'explanation' as used substitutes one familiar mystery for another; explaining a law by another law does not remove the ultimate mystery of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'explanation' instrumentally: explanations improve familiarity and show relations among laws and extend deductive reach, but they do not necessarily answer metaphysical 'why' questions about ultimate causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of deduction when many unknown or unquantified causes interact
rubrics_metrics.description: When a multitude (often unknown) of agencies are clashing and combining, deductive computations may be insecure because we may have omitted causes or lack accurate numerical laws for each; even when included, calculations may exceed mathematical capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise caution in claiming a priori computations for complex phenomena (e.g., physiological, mental, social phenomena). Use verification and simpler instances to check deductions; avoid overreliance on deduction where numerical laws and feasible computation are absent.
